newsitem.title: USA: Sales of new homes ease down in February.
newsitem.headline: Sales of new homes ease down in February.

text.p: Sales of new U.S. homes fell slightly last month after a January surge, the Commerce Department said Friday, despite cheaper mortgages and favorable weather.

Sales fell 0.7 percent during February to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 811,000 units after a sharply revised 3.5 percent gain in January to 817,000. Previously, the department said January sales had jumped 8.6 percent to 870,000.
The February falloff in new-home sales was the first in four months in four months, since an 8.1 percent drop last October.
Nonetheless, February sales were still 3.5 percent above levels a year earlier, in February 1996 when sales were at a rate of 778,000.

In addition, the supply of new homes for sale declined to the lowest in more than three years, down to 4.6 months' worth from 4.8 months in January. The last time there was a smaller supply of homes available was in December 1993 when 4.5 months' worth were on the market.

A department official said the January revision -- to a sales level of 817,000 from 870,000 -- was within its normal range. The department is in the process of changings its collection method for new-home sales, using laptop computers instead of pencil and paper to record datat, and will complete the transition by July, it said.
The January sales pace remained the strongest since April 1986 when they were selling at a rate of 857,000 a year.

The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. said rates for a 30-year mortgage loan averaged 7.65 percent in February, down from 7.82 percent in January. But it was higher than the 7.08 percent mortgage rate available a year earlier in February 1996.
The housing industry retains plenty of momentum, despite the slight backing off in February sales of new homes.

On Thursday, the National Association of Realtors said sales of existing, or previously occupied, homes shot up to the second highest level on record last month as a growing economy boosted buyer activity.
The industry lobby group said sales of existing homes rose 9.0 percent in February to a seasonably adjusted annual rate of 4.26 million units from a revised 3.91 million units in January.
For new homes, the only region where February sales increased was the West, where they rose 11.7 percent to an annual rate of 210,000.
In the Northeast, sales dropped 11.2 percent to 95,000 a year during February and in the Midwest they were down 3.4 percent to 141,000.
Sales also fell in February by 3.4 percent in the South, the nation's biggest housing market, to 364,000 a year.

The average home sales price in February climbed to $174,500 from $170,200 in January. But the median sales price -- with half the homes selling above this level and half selling below --was down to $143,200 from $143,800.
